obstacle_assessment.reasoning: The coordinate-module claims follow from the matrix-unit decomposition and elementary finite-module calculations; no substantive defect remains.

complete_proof: Put R=Z_(p), n=lambda+1, and e_i=y^i v/i! for 0<=i<=lambda. The supplied sl2 relations and highest-weight equations, iterated, give X_r e_i=binom(lambda-i+r,r)e_(i-r) and Y_r e_i=binom(i+r,r)e_(i+r), with out-of-range vectors zero, where X_r=x^r/r! and Y_r=y^r/r!. For matrix units E_ab this gives Y_lambda X_lambda=E_lambda,lambda, X_(lambda-i)E_lambda,lambda=E_i,lambda, and E_lambda,lambda Y_(lambda-j)=binom(lambda,j)E_lambda,j. The last coefficient is a unit of R because lambda<p. Hence every E_i,j=E_i,lambda E_lambda,j is in the R-algebra generated by divided powers and preserves M_R=R tensor_Z M by admissibility. Define J_i={c in C:c e_i in M_R}. The module M_R is finite free; E_ii(M_R)=J_i e_i, so J_i is finitely generated. It is nonzero since M_R spans the complex module and E_ii is nonzero. Applying E_ij to c e_j shows J_j subset J_i; reversing the indices gives equality. Call the common module J. Projecting any m in M_R by each E_ii shows its coordinates lie in J e_i, while the definition of J gives the reverse inclusion. Thus M_R=direct_sum_i J e_i. Localize at the fraction field Q of R. Since M_R has rank n, the decomposition gives n=n dim_Q(Q tensor_R J), so J has rank one. J is torsion-free as a submodule of C. Choose a Q-linear identification of Q tensor_R J with Q; its image I of J is a nonzero finitely generated R-submodule of Q. Clearing denominators gives a nonzero finitely generated ideal dI of R. Each nonzero q in Q has form p^k u with integer k and u a unit of R. For any nonzero finitely generated ideal, take the least exponent k among a finite set of nonzero generators: all generators lie in p^k R and one is p^k times a unit, so the ideal is p^k R. Thus dI is principal and J is free of rank one. Choose a generator a; then a e_i form an R-basis of M_R. On this basis x(ae_i)=(lambda-i+1)ae_(i-1), y(ae_i)=(i+1)ae_(i+1), and h(ae_i)=(lambda-2i)ae_i, with out-of-range terms zero. Reduction modulo p therefore gives the standard module. Also M_R/pM_R is M tensor_Z F_p: a Z-basis of M gives the same reduced basis and reduced integral action matrices. Extending scalars from F_p to K gives an L(K)-module isomorphism with the standard module over K. For r<=lambda<p, r! is invertible modulo p, so X_r and Y_r are scalar multiples of powers of x and y. The matrix-unit identities remain valid modulo p since binom(lambda,j) is nonzero there. Any K-subspace W invariant under x,y,h is invariant under every E_i,j. If w=sum_i c_i e_i is a nonzero vector in W, choose i with c_i nonzero. Then E_ji w=c_i e_j for every j, so every basis vector belongs to W and W is the whole module. Its dimension lambda+1 is positive. This proves the result, including lambda=0, without requiring p>2 or distinct reduced h-weights.
source_obligations: No literature theorem is imported. The divided-power formulas follow by iteration from the supplied sl2 relations and highest-weight equations. Matrix-unit identities and R-module arguments are derived in the proof. The characteristic-zero basis and dimension, lattice properties, and action setup are supplied by the frozen context and hypotheses.
edge_cases: lambda=0 gives a one-dimensional module with identity matrix unit. For p=2, lambda is 0 or 1; no division by 2 occurs. The proof treats every admissible lattice and every field K of characteristic p by extension from F_p.
